{{< include /knowledge/includes/setup-parameters.qmd >}}

The companies that lobby your government to build infinity bombs and spend {{< var military_to_government_clinical_trials_spending_ratio_nounit >}} dollars on mass-murder capacity for every dollar on curing diseases that are {{< var annual_terrorism_death_risk_denominator_nounit >}} times more likely to kill you than a terrorist are publicly traded. Anyone can buy their shares. Each share carries a vote for the board of directors. The board tells the lobbyists what to say. This is how you change what they say, what it costs, and what happens to your income and lifespan when you do.

## The Problem

Governments spend {{< var military_to_government_clinical_trials_spending_ratio_nounit >}} dollars on the military for every dollar they spend on clinical trials. Disease kills {{< var disease_vs_war_deaths_ratio_nounit >}} people for every person war kills. {{< var diseases_without_effective_treatment >}} have no effective treatment, because the trials that would find one are not funded.

The world holds {{< var global_warhead_count >}}. About {{< var nuclear_winter_warhead_threshold >}} are enough to start a nuclear winter and end civilization once. The arsenal is {{< var nuclear_winter_overkill_factor_nounit >}} times that size. There is one civilization to end. [The Apocalypse Markup](extinction-surplus.qmd) prices the extra copies.

Deterrence does not require this. A survivable nuclear force, about 100 to 200 warheads on submarines, costs about {{< var us_defense_fp_nuclear_deterrent >}} a year. Add missile defense, the Coast Guard, the National Guard, and cyber protection, and the full cost of defending the United States is about {{< var us_defense_first_principles_optimal >}} a year. [The first-principles breakdown](cost-benefit-of-hegemony.qmd) prices each component. The United States spends {{< var us_military_spending_2024_annual >}}. In 1939 it spent {{< var us_military_spending_1939_annual_2024usd >}} in today's dollars. Today, at {{< var us_military_spending_current_vs_prewar_multiplier >}} that, it cannot keep a shipping lane open against a militia with drones. The difference between the {{< var us_defense_first_principles_optimal >}} that homeland defense costs and the {{< var us_military_spending_2024_annual >}} it actually spends is {{< var us_gov_waste_military_overspend >}} a year in weapons above deterrence. [The Cost-Benefit Analysis of Global Hegemony](cost-benefit-of-hegemony.qmd) audits what the difference buys.

## How Lobbying Produces It

Nobody voted for {{< var military_to_government_clinical_trials_spending_ratio_nounit >}} to 1. It is the output of a chain. Each link is a person maximizing their short-term income at the expense of their own eventual suffering and death, and that of everyone they have ever loved.

1. Military contractors pay lobbyists {{< var defense_lobbying_annual >}} a year.
2. The lobbyists tell Congress to buy enough bombs for {{< var nuclear_winter_overkill_factor_nounit >}} apocalypses even though there is one civilization to apocalypse.
3. Congress buys them. Over the twenty years of the Afghanistan war, the five biggest military contractors spent $1.1 billion on lobbying and received $2.02 trillion in contracts. That is $1,813 back for every dollar spent [@lobbying-roi-calc].
4. A Princeton study of 1,779 policy decisions found that organized business groups get the policies they lobby for and the preferences of average citizens have almost no effect [@gilens2014]. [Unrepresentative Democracy](../problem/unrepresentative-democracy.qmd) has the details.
5. Every dollar that buys a bomb is a dollar that does not test a treatment for the diseases that are {{< var annual_terrorism_death_risk_denominator_nounit >}} times more likely to kill you than a terrorist.
6. Each contractor's board of directors approves the lobbying budget and the message.
7. Shareholders elect the board.

So the lobbying message belongs to whoever holds the shares. Nobody in the chain is evil. [There Are No Bad Guys](../proof/no-bad-guys.qmd) has the proof. The last link is the cheapest one to change. Change it and the other six follow.

## The World That Could Be

The boards tell the same lobbyists to argue for the budget that doubles median after-tax income to {{< var treaty_trajectory_median_after_tax_income_year_20 >}} and adds {{< var avg_life_extension_per_beneficiary >}} healthy years per person who benefits. The [Optimal Budget Generator](optimal-budget-generator-spec.qmd) [@obg-paper-2025] looks at what 10,000 jurisdictions actually spent, what happened to their citizens, and calculates the allocation that would have produced the best outcomes. Its first instruction is the [1% treaty](../solution/1-percent-treaty.qmd) [@1-pct-treaty-impact-paper-2025] [@1-percent-treaty-paper-2025]: move 1 percent of military spending to clinical trials. The other {{< var defense_sector_retention_pct >}} stays where it is.

1. The lobbyists sell Congress the treaty the same way they sell weapons. Same people, same phone numbers. The sentence changes from "buy more bombs" to "move 1 percent to clinical trials."
2. The treaty passes. {{< var treaty_annual_funding >}} a year moves from weapons to trials.
3. The trials run on the diseases that have no treatment, through a [decentralized trial system](../solution/dfda.qmd) [@dfda-spec-paper-2025] that cuts the cost per patient by {{< var dfda_trial_cost_reduction_pct >}}.
4. Treatments arrive for the {{< var diseases_without_effective_treatment >}} that have none today. Millions of people who were going to die stop dying. Each one starts earning instead of costing.
5. At year 15, world GDP is {{< var treaty_trajectory_gdp_vs_current_trajectory_multiplier_year_15 >}} what it would be on the current path. Over a lifetime, the median person gains {{< var treaty_trajectory_lifetime_income_gain_per_capita >}} in after-tax income and {{< var avg_life_extension_per_beneficiary >}} healthy years. The [full model](../economics/1-pct-treaty-impact.qmd) [@1-pct-treaty-impact-paper-2025] shows every assumption.

What the median person gets:

| | Current path | Treaty path |
|---|---:|---:|
| Median after-tax income at year 20 | {{< var current_trajectory_median_after_tax_income_year_20 >}} | {{< var treaty_trajectory_median_after_tax_income_year_20 >}} |
| Lifetime income gain per person | | {{< var treaty_trajectory_lifetime_income_gain_per_capita >}} |
| Extra healthy years per person who benefits | | {{< var avg_life_extension_per_beneficiary >}} |

A military contractor's revenue is a share of the military budget. If the economy is {{< var treaty_trajectory_gdp_vs_current_trajectory_multiplier_year_15 >}} larger, the budget is larger in dollars at the same share of GDP, so revenue rises without winning a single new contract. The engineers who build guidance systems can build diagnostic instruments, and net margins in pharmaceuticals are {{< var pharma_vs_defense_net_margin_ratio >}} the net margins in weapons. And the directors are people. They get the same treatments as everyone else.

Nobody loses. Existing shareholders keep their shares, and the shares are worth more, because an economy {{< var treaty_trajectory_gdp_vs_current_trajectory_multiplier_year_15 >}} larger means a larger budget at the same share of GDP. Employees keep their jobs; {{< var defense_sector_retention_pct >}} of the budget stays. Directors who cooperate keep their seats. The only thing that changes is what the lobbyists say.

## How to Do It

### Form a holding company

Berkshire Hathaway buys shares in other companies and holds them. Yours buys shares in military contractors. The [Earth Optimization Fund](../economics/earth-optimization-fund.qmd) page has the legal structure; you can copy it.

### Buy a stake

You do not need a majority. Each tier gets you something.

| Stake | What it gets you | Cost across the big Western military contractors |
|---|---|---:|
| One share | A [letter the board must read](love-letter.qmd), and the right to [sue the directors](lawsuit.qmd) if they ignore it | About $200 |
| Under 1 percent, plus a campaign | Board seats, if the index funds vote with you | $75 million to $200 million |
| 1 to 5 percent | An agenda item at every annual meeting | $10 billion to $48 billion |
| 50.1 percent | Nobody has to agree with you | {{< var defense_takeover_cost_total >}} |

Start with one share. The letter is written, with [eight pre-filled versions](pre-filled-demand-letters.qmd), one per contractor. If the board ignores it for 60 days, the next step is a [shareholder proposal](shareholder-proposal-14a-8.qmd) on the annual ballot.

### Write the case for the index funds

Three index-fund managers, Vanguard, BlackRock, and State Street, hold roughly 20 to 30 percent of every big military contractor. Institutions together hold 70 to 85 percent. The companies' own proxy statements list them. Their job is to vote for whatever makes their portfolio worth more.

Their portfolio is the whole economy. If one contractor sells more missiles, the fund gains on one holding. If the whole economy is {{< var treaty_trajectory_gdp_vs_current_trajectory_multiplier_year_15 >}} larger because millions of sick people are earning instead of dying, the fund gains on every holding it has. {{< var treaty_trajectory_lifetime_income_gain_per_capita >}} in extra lifetime income per person, multiplied by billions of people, is worth more to the fund than any missile contract. You do not need to buy the index funds. You need to show them this arithmetic with the [model](../economics/1-pct-treaty-impact.qmd) attached.

Do not form a voting pact with them. Funds that agree to vote together can become a "group" under securities law, with disclosure duties. Make the case in public. Let each fund vote its own interest.

### Replace the board and hand over the budget

When you have the votes, elect directors who hand the lobbyists new instructions. The [Optimitron](../solution/optimocracy.qmd) analyzes outcome data from roughly 10,000 jurisdictions that already tried different policy allocations and finds the budget that actually maximized median healthy lifespan and median after-tax income. The [Optimal Budget Generator](optimal-budget-generator-spec.qmd) [@obg-paper-2025] is the specification; the [legislation package](../strategy/legislation-package.qmd) is the bill text it produces. The lobbyists keep their jobs and their contacts. They argue for the budget that makes their client richer, which is now also the budget that keeps their client's customers, employees, and directors alive.

### Repeat

Start with the smallest contractor. Each win makes the next one cheaper, because the index funds have seen the argument work. When the military contractors are done, the [same procedure](../economics/earth-optimization-fund.qmd) applies to every other industry that pays lobbyists to make its own shareholders sicker or poorer.

## Precedents

**The bomb budget has been cut before.** The United States cut military spending by {{< var post_ww2_military_cut_pct >}} after World War 2 in two years. The largest rise in living standards in its history followed. [They Cut the Bomb Budget 87% and Everyone Got Richer](../proof/bomb-budget-cut.qmd) has the story.

**A small stake has replaced a board before.** In May 2021, Engine No. 1 held about $40 million of ExxonMobil, 0.02 percent of the company. It nominated four directors and argued Exxon was betting its shareholders' money on oil the world was moving away from. The big index funds voted with it. Three of the four nominees won seats [@engine-no-1-exxon-2021]. Engine No. 1 did not need to own Exxon. It needed a case the index funds accepted.

**The lobby itself proves the lever works.** {{< var defense_lobbying_annual >}} a year of lobbying has kept United States military spending at {{< var us_military_spending_2024_annual >}}, {{< var us_military_spending_current_vs_prewar_multiplier >}} the prewar budget, and buried every serious reallocation proposal since the 1960s. Same machine, different sentence.

## What It Costs

### The ceiling: buy everything outright

Approximate market caps of the big Western military contractors, June 2026:

| Contractor | Ticker | Approx market cap | 50%+1 control cost |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| RTX (Raytheon) | RTX | ~$248B | ~$124B |
| Boeing | BA | ~$175B | ~$87B |
| Lockheed Martin | LMT | ~$127B | ~$63B |
| General Dynamics | GD | ~$97B | ~$49B |
| Northrop Grumman | NOC | ~$79B | ~$39B |
| L3Harris | LHX | ~$58B | ~$29B |
| Leidos | LDOS | ~$15B | ~$8B |
| Huntington Ingalls | HII | ~$12B | ~$6B |
| CACI International | CACI | ~$12B | ~$6B |
| Booz Allen Hamilton | BAH | ~$9B | ~$5B |
| SAIC | SAIC | ~$5B | ~$2.5B |
| **US subtotal** | | **~$836B** | **~$419B** |
| BAE Systems (UK) | BA.L | ~$76B | ~$38B |
| Thales (France) | HO.PA | ~$57B | ~$28B |
| **Allied subtotal** | | **~$132B** | **~$66B** |
| **Total** | | **~$968B** | **~$485B** |

Buying 50.1 percent of all of them, with a {{< var defense_takeover_acquisition_premium >}} premium, costs about {{< var defense_takeover_cost_total >}}. Spread across {{< var global_population_2024_nounit >}} people, that is {{< var defense_takeover_cost_per_human >}} per person. Governments spend {{< var us_military_spending_2024_annual >}} on the US military alone every year, {{< var us_military_spending_current_vs_prewar_multiplier >}} what won World War 2.

| Cost spread across | Per person |
|---|---:|
| Everyone on Earth ({{< var global_population_2024_nounit >}}) | **~{{< var defense_takeover_cost_per_human >}}** |
| Adults (~5.5 billion) | ~$160 |
| Middle class and above (~3.5 billion) | ~$250 |
| US adults (260 million) | ~$3,400 |
| US households (130 million) | ~$6,700 |
| US households earning over $100k (~50 million) | ~$17,500 |

Against the {{< var defense_takeover_cost_per_human >}}: the treaty path adds {{< var treaty_trajectory_lifetime_income_gain_per_capita >}} in lifetime income and {{< var avg_life_extension_per_beneficiary >}} healthy years per person who benefits. The income alone is {{< var defense_takeover_roi_income_only >}} the cost. With the healthy years, {{< var defense_takeover_roi_income_plus_health >}}.

### The plan: campaigns with the index funds' votes

A campaign that wins board seats with the index funds' votes costs $75 million to $200 million across all the big Western contractors. Engine No. 1 did it at ExxonMobil for $40 million. The first letter costs one share, about $200.

You could instead [buy the politicians directly](cost-of-change-analysis.qmd), for about {{< var us_political_reform_investment_total >}} in the United States. That money is spent, and it must be spent again every election. Shares are an asset. If the campaign fails, you still own them.
